newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Pound, strike hit BA's profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Pound, strike hit BA's profits.

text.p: British Airways Plc warned on Monday that profits were taking a battering from the strength of sterling this year and last month's cabin crew strike would cost it a further 125 million pounds ($203.8 million), far above share market estimates.
BA shares fell on the news as the company reported first half results and analysts moved to cut profit forecasts. The shares closed down 29-1/2p at 610-1/2.
"It is a straight fact that our sales in foreign currency are worth less in sterling and this outweighs foreign currency costs like fuel (priced in dollars)," BA finance director Derek Stevens said.

Headline profits for the first quarter ended June 30 jumped 46.7 percent to 220 million pounds, thanks to an exceptional gain of 130 million pounds from the sale of its stake in former U.S. partner US Air.

But the airline said operating profits for the three months dropped 55 million pounds ($89.7 million) to 140 million pounds, despite a 5.4 percent rise in turnover to 2.22 billion pounds. BA shares dropped 21 pence to 619 after touching a low of 611.

Adding to its woes, BA said it was still hopeful it could win approval for its proposed alliance with American Airlines but it has drawn up contingency plans in case the deal should be blocked by the European or U.S. regulatory authorities.
Sterling's strength depressed the headline result by 77 million pounds while the beginnings of industrial unrest cost 15 million pounds in lost revenue and contingency moves in the quarter.
And BA warned the subsequent three-day strike by cabin crew which grounded hundreds of flights was likely to wipe 110 million off profits in the second quarter.

Management negotiators are still locked in talks with the main cabin crew union, BASSA, in an effort to settle the dispute over plans to save 42 million pounds a year from restructuring cabin crew pay.
BA said that elsewhere in the group efforts to cut a billion pounds off annual costs by 2000 were running to plan, with 200 million pounds of the target expected to be achieved in the current year.

Analysts expressed surprise at the size of the impact of both sterling and the industrial dispute on profits as well by an increase in underlying costs, and said they would reduce full-year forecasts.
Chris Gunn at Credit Lyonnais Laing said he expected current year pre-tax profit estimates before exceptional items to come down to between 500 and 510 million pounds from 580-600 million.

Gunn said BA was facing a rising tax charge and heavy capital spending, as well as higher-than-expected currency and strike costs. "For the first time in ages, BA looks as if it is on the back foot," he said.

Analysts had been pencilling in between 50 and 100 million for the industrial dispute and 100 million for exchange rates. Now the impact of sterling could be at least double that figure, Chris Avery of Paribas said.

Total BA traffic for the three months to June 30 rose 7.8 percent and capacity by 6.7 percent with an average 73 percent of all seats sold on every flight, an increase of 0.7 percentage points on a year ago.

The average fare paid fell 2.4 percent to 6.44 pence per passenger for every kilometre flown, which the airline said was "more than explained" by the increased strength of sterling. But unit costs rose 0.4 percent and would have been up 4.6 percent had it not been for the effects of exchange rates on foreign currency costs.

On the American tie-up, BA has already threatened to abandon the deal if approvals are not granted before November, having struggled for more than a year to agree terms with the European and U.S. competition authorities.

"There are always fallback alternatives and obviously we have our contingency plans but a deal with American would certainly be the most attractive in the commercial sense, depending on the regulatory price," finance director Derek Stevens told Reuters.
"If the regulators are going to make it too expensive to do then of course we have to look at alternatives," he said. "There has to be a time limit on this," he added.

Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT) proposed last December that BA and American should release 168 weekly runway slots at Heathrow -- enough to operate 12 daily return flights -- to give other airlines room to compete.

But industry sources say the European Union's competition Commissioner has suggested to BA and the OFT that it should release 350 weekly slots at Heathrow, far more than BA would ever be willing to give up. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
